title: Every best gift (James 1:17)
hook: every good gift comes from the Father of lights

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last chapter of Hebrews: welcome strangers. Your line was angels unawares. Whose name did you learn? Day six hundred four.

A sundial works only because the light keeps moving. Morning shadows stretch long to the west, shrink to almost nothing at noon, and swing around to the east by evening. The sun is faithful, but it never holds still, and everything it touches casts a shadow that turns. Winter days are short, summer days are long, clouds come and go. Today we open a new letter, the letter of James, and in its first chapter James looks up at that moving sky and says something about the one who made it.
screen: `A SUNDIAL NEEDS MOVING LIGHT.` → `EVERY SHADOW TURNS.` → `A NEW LETTER: JAMES.`

segments.voice: The letter opens simply: James, the servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes scattered abroad. Which James? The letter doesn't say. Many in the early Church held it was James of Jerusalem, called the brother of the Lord, and Catholic tradition has often identified him with James the Less, one of the twelve. Scholars still discuss it. Then, almost at once, James talks about trials and temptation. And he draws a firm line. When someone is tempted, they shouldn't say God is tempting them. God tempts no one. Temptation grows from our own desires. So where does God come in? Here, in the Douay-Rheims: "Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration." Father of lights. Many readers hear the lights of Genesis one here: the sun, the moon, the stars, which God made. Those lights move. They wax and wane, rise and set, and the shadows they cast turn all day long. God doesn't. With him, James says, there's no shadow of alteration. The good he gives isn't a passing mood that will swing around by evening. And the very next verse names the greatest gift: of his own will God has brought us to birth by the word of truth. Put it together and the line becomes a habit of attention. The good things in a life, the friend, the meal, the recovery, the morning, have a source, and James traces them up.
screen: `WHICH JAMES? THE LETTER DOESN'T SAY.` · `GOD TEMPTS NO ONE.` · `THE FATHER OF LIGHTS.` · `NO SHADOW OF ALTERATION.` · then, large: `EVERY BEST GIFT IS FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank God for one gift. Sit comfortably near a window if you can, and notice where the light is falling right now. Breathe. Then choose one good thing from the past day. Something specific: a conversation, a warm meal, a task that went right, a body that carried you around. Hold it in mind as if it had just been handed to you. Trace it up, step by step: who made it possible, and who made them possible. If you pray, you can thank God for it by name, the way James would trace it back to the Father of lights. If you don't, just let yourself be grateful. The bell holds the time.
Every best gift. James one seventeen: every good and perfect gift comes from above, from the Father of lights, who doesn't change. Today's word.
Your line: from above. Today, when something good happens, even something small, stop for one breath and say from above. Day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics give thanks for God's gifts in grace before meals, in the thanksgiving after Communion, and in the Mass itself, whose name Eucharist comes from the Greek for thanksgiving.

fork.reveal: James draws the line firmly: God tempts no one. then he turns it around. what comes from God is every best gift.

original.note: Greek: from above (James 1:17). John 3 uses the same word for being born from above.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice line for a thank-you card.
what it means: James traces every good thing to God, who, unlike the shifting lights in the sky, doesn't change.
what a scholar hears: Father of lights, the maker of the heavenly bodies of Genesis 1. their shadows turn; with God there's no shadow of alteration.

sources.quoted: Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration.

notes: Authorship of James: the script says many in the early Church held it was James of Jerusalem, the brother of the Lord, and that Catholic tradition has often identified him with James the Less (son of Alphaeus). Confirm the wording is fair to the Catholic tradition and to current scholarship.
'Father of lights' read as the maker of the heavenly lights of Genesis 1 is presented as how many readers hear it. Confirm.
James 1:13–15 (God tempts no one) and 1:18 (begotten by the word of truth) are paraphrased.
ἄνωθεν in James 1:17 and John 3:3: confirm the same word.
